stories.headline: Colorado income tax overhaul targeting top earners heads to November ballot
stories.summary:
Colorado voters will decide this November whether to replace the state's flat 4.4% income tax rate with a graduated system under Initiative 195. Individuals and businesses earning more than $500,000 annually would pay higher rates, while roughly 97% of Coloradans would see a tax reduction averaging $210 for those earning $50,000 to $100,000 per year.

The nonpartisan Legislative Council Staff estimates the measure would increase state revenue by approximately $2 billion annually by fiscal year 2027-28, with a projected maximum of $2.7 billion. Supporters say those funds would be directed toward K-12 education, healthcare, and childcare programs, including Medicaid services cut by the federal government.

Opponents, including Advance Colorado President Michael Fields, argue the change could drive high-income earners and businesses to lower-tax states such as Florida or Wyoming, potentially reducing overall tax revenue. The Independence Institute also raised concerns that the additional revenue would be exempt from the state's TABOR revenue cap.

A competing measure, Initiative 232, backed by Advance Colorado, would cap the state income tax rate at 4.4%. Under state law, if both initiatives pass, the one receiving the most "yes" votes takes effect.

stories.headline: 8th Congressional District voters favor lighter immigration enforcement, poll finds
stories.summary:
Voters in Colorado's 8th Congressional District — covering parts of Weld, Larimer and Adams counties north of Denver — overwhelmingly favor a less aggressive approach to immigration enforcement than the Trump administration's current strategy of raids and mass deportations, according to a poll released by the University of Maryland's School of Public Policy.

The survey of 500 district voters conducted in May and June found broad bipartisan agreement on several immigration questions, including support for pathways to citizenship for DACA recipients and employer verification requirements. The 8th District has the highest concentration of Latino residents among Colorado's eight congressional districts.

Republican incumbent Rep. Gabe Evans has sought to differentiate himself from the administration on immigration, joining a bipartisan letter to ICE leadership last year questioning enforcement priorities. His Democratic challenger, state Rep. Manny Rutinel, has made criticism of ICE tactics a central theme of his campaign.

The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up. Analysts note that Trump's immigration posture could prove a particular liability for Evans given the district's demographics.

stories.headline: 377,000 Coloradans notified of new Medicaid work requirements taking effect in January
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Health Care Policy and Financing has begun sending letters, emails and texts to an estimated 377,000 Medicaid recipients warning them of new federal work requirements that take effect Jan. 1, 2027. The rules, part of the federal "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," require proof of work or "community engagement" of at least 80 hours per month to maintain coverage.

Those affected are individuals earning $20,815 or less per year, or families of four earning $42,760 or less. The new rules also require beneficiaries to verify eligibility every six months instead of annually. Exemptions apply to people who are pregnant, under 18, over 65, or caring for a young child or a family member with a disability.

State Medicaid officials stressed that not everyone receiving a letter will necessarily be subject to the requirements, but urged recipients not to ignore the notices. Those who fail to demonstrate compliance or exemption status risk losing their Health First Colorado coverage.

Colorado's Medicaid program covers approximately 1.1 million residents. The new requirements come on top of state-level cuts to programs for people with disabilities and low incomes made earlier this year as lawmakers addressed a $1.5 billion budget shortfall.

stories.headline: Barry Morphew placed on full-time house arrest after alleged Denver hit-and-run
stories.summary:
Barry Morphew, who is awaiting trial on charges of murdering his wife Suzanne Morphew, has been placed under full-time house arrest after a judge found he violated his conditional release conditions. Alamosa District Court Judge Amanda Hopkins issued the order after reviewing video of an Aug. 26 hit-and-run and road rage incident near East 8th Avenue and Colorado Boulevard in Denver.

A woman involved in the Denver hit-and-run told CBS Colorado she believes Morphew was the driver who struck her vehicle. A source close to the Morphew family who viewed the video also told the outlet he was certain the man depicted was Barry Morphew. Denver police have not officially confirmed the driver's identity.

Morphew had previously been released on conditions while awaiting trial in the high-profile case involving the 2020 disappearance and death of his wife. The house arrest order was issued less than a day after CBS Colorado's initial report on the incident.

The case has drawn sustained public attention since Suzanne Morphew's remains were discovered in Chaffee County. Barry Morphew faces first-degree murder charges in connection with her death.

stories.headline: 14-year-old Denver boy arrested on attempted murder charge in Sand Creek Park shooting
stories.summary:
A 14-year-old boy from Denver was arrested early Sunday morning in connection with a shooting at Sand Creek Park in northwest Aurora that left one man injured, Aurora police reported. The teen faces charges of attempted first-degree murder, aggravated assault, reckless endangerment, and possession of a handgun by a juvenile.

Aurora police did not release additional details about the circumstances of the shooting or the condition of the victim. The arrest follows a string of high-profile violent incidents involving juveniles in the Denver metro area in recent weeks.

The Sand Creek Park shooting is separate from other recent Denver-area incidents, including a Wednesday shooting near the Denver School of the Arts in which three people were hospitalized. Denver police are still investigating that case and working to identify suspects.

Juvenile gun violence has been a persistent concern for law enforcement agencies across the metro area, and the charges filed against the 14-year-old represent some of the most serious that can be brought against a minor under Colorado law.

stories.headline: 3 people hospitalized after shooting near Denver School of the Arts
stories.summary:
Three people were injured and hospitalized after a shooting near the Denver School of the Arts, the Denver Police Department announced Wednesday. Police are investigating the incident and working to identify potential suspects, according to a department social media post.

Few additional details were immediately available about the circumstances of the shooting or the conditions of the victims. The location near a Denver public school drew particular attention from community members and city officials.

The shooting is one of several violent incidents reported across the Denver metro area in recent days, including the Sand Creek Park shooting in Aurora in which a 14-year-old Denver boy was arrested. Law enforcement agencies have been responding to an elevated number of shooting calls this summer.

Denver police asked anyone with information about the School of the Arts shooting to contact investigators.

stories.headline: Denver police issue guidance on how to handle Waymo driverless cars during stops and crashes
stories.summary:
The Denver Police Department distributed a training bulletin in early July detailing how officers should interact with Waymo autonomous vehicles, which formally launched public service in Denver on Tuesday. The memo, obtained by BusinessDen, explains that Waymo cars are designed to pull over when they detect emergency lights, then unlock doors and lower windows so a Waymo representative can communicate with officers via phone.

Because Colorado state law currently lacks a mechanism to issue traffic citations when no human driver is present, Waymo vehicles cannot be ticketed under existing statutes. Officers can also use QR codes on the vehicle windows or a dispatch button on the center console to reach Waymo staff.

The bulletin addresses several edge cases, including erratic vehicle behavior, fires — which may release toxic vapors and should not be extinguished by officers unless necessary for an immediate life-saving rescue — and crash reporting, which requires leaving the driver information section blank and noting the vehicle as self-driving. A search warrant is required to obtain passenger history or interior camera footage, which is otherwise deleted after 24 hours.

Waymo has been involved in one local collision, in which a vehicle was rear-ended near Denver Health along Eighth Avenue last week. The company says it was not at fault and reports all qualifying collisions to federal regulators under a standing general order.

stories.headline: Rapids sell Rafael Navarro to St. Louis City for MLS-record $12 million
stories.summary:
The Colorado Rapids set a new MLS record Wednesday by selling striker Rafael Navarro to St. Louis City SC for $12 million, the highest cash transfer fee between two MLS clubs in league history. Navarro, 26, had been one of the team's most consistent offensive players since arriving on loan from Brazilian club Palmeiras in 2023, finishing with 44 goals and 12 assists in 114 appearances.

The Rapids had already secured his replacement, signing Sayed Abu Farkhi from Israeli Premier League side Maccabi Tel Aviv for approximately $6 million. Homegrown striker Darren Yapi is also expected to compete for playing time with Navarro's departure. The move allows Colorado to redirect resources to other roster areas under coach Matt Wells.

Rapids president Pádraig Smith acknowledged the difficulty of the decision but said it was the right move for both the club and the player. Coach Wells called Navarro "an outstanding player and an even better person," adding that he has the mentality of the world's best.

Navarro had become a fan favorite in Colorado, highlighted by a solo run against Lionel Messi and Inter Miami at Empower Field at Mile High this season. His departure comes as the Rapids continue to shape their roster around Wells' tactical system ahead of the stretch run of the MLS season.

stories.headline: Sean Payton defends Bo Nix against critics, names Jarrett Stidham as backup quarterback
stories.summary:
Broncos head coach Sean Payton addressed ongoing skepticism about second-year quarterback Bo Nix on Wednesday, pushing back against analysts and media figures who have questioned Nix's development. Payton suggested critics are either slow to update their draft-era opinions or lack sufficient exposure to the quarterback during games and practice.

Nix was notably absent from ESPN's list of the top 100 players in the NFL heading into the 2026 season, though five other Broncos made the list, including cornerback Pat Surtain II at No. 7. Veteran tight end Evan Engram said the team gives "no energy" to outside opinions and expressed confidence in their quarterback.

Payton also clarified the backup quarterback situation, confirming that Jarrett Stidham is currently the No. 2 behind Nix, ahead of Sam Ehlinger, who made the 53-man roster. The coach had been noncommittal on that question following the preseason finale.

On the subject of veteran tight end Taysom Hill, who was released by New Orleans earlier this offseason, Payton said he spoke with Hill at Drew Brees' Hall of Fame induction ceremony but that no signing discussions are underway. "I kind of like where we're at," Payton said of Denver's current tight end room.

stories.headline: Nuggets sign DeMar DeRozan, adding six-time All-Star to roster alongside Jokić and Murray
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets have signed DeMar DeRozan, a six-time NBA All-Star, adding a proven veteran scorer to a team that already features two-time MVP Nikola Jokić and All-Star guard Jamal Murray. The signing gives Denver one of the most experienced offensive trios in the Western Conference heading into the 2026-27 season.

DeRozan, known for his mid-range scoring ability and shot creation, spent recent seasons with Chicago and Sacramento before joining Denver. His addition addresses the Nuggets' need for a reliable secondary scorer and shot creator who can operate in pick-and-roll and isolation situations alongside Jokić.

The move signals Denver's intention to remain a championship contender after falling short in recent playoff runs. Team officials and coaching staff have not yet commented publicly on how DeRozan will be integrated into head coach Michael Malone's offensive system.

The Nuggets open the 2026-27 regular season in October. DeRozan's signing is expected to draw immediate attention from around the league as Denver looks to challenge for a return to the NBA Finals.

stories.headline: Edgewater restaurants navigate Colorado's new tipped wage law with cautious optimism
stories.summary:
Restaurant operators in Edgewater are reporting mixed early results from Colorado's updated tipped wage law, which took effect this year and altered how employers calculate minimum pay for tipped workers. Some owners say the change has provided modest financial relief and reduced turnover, while others describe ongoing uncertainty about long-term cost impacts.

Colorado's tipped wage rules have been a subject of significant debate between labor advocates, who argue tipped workers deserve greater wage stability, and restaurant industry groups, which warn that higher mandatory base pay could force menu price increases, staffing cuts or closures. Edgewater, a small city bordering west Denver, offered a concentrated look at how the changes are playing out in real businesses.

Some restaurateurs said the law has made it easier to recruit and retain staff, reducing the volatility that comes from relying heavily on customer gratuities. Others expressed concern about what happens during slower seasons when tip income naturally drops and the mandated base wage puts added pressure on margins.

The findings from Edgewater are being watched by restaurant operators and policymakers across the metro area as Colorado continues to adjust its wage framework. Industry groups say more data from a full year of operation under the new rules will be needed before drawing firm conclusions.

stories.headline: Death of Englewood mayor pro tem on Quandary Peak prompts review of high-altitude medical warnings
stories.summary:
The death of Englewood Mayor Pro Tem on Quandary Peak, one of Colorado's 14,000-foot summits, has prompted a review of high-altitude medical warning systems and communications for hikers attempting the state's most popular fourteeners. Officials and medical experts are examining whether existing warnings about altitude sickness and cardiac risk are sufficient for the volume of hikers who attempt high-altitude peaks each year.

Quandary Peak near Breckenridge is among the most heavily trafficked fourteeners in Colorado, drawing thousands of hikers annually, including many with limited high-altitude experience. Medical professionals note that altitude-related illness can affect even physically fit individuals and that symptoms can escalate quickly above 12,000 feet.

The Englewood official's death has drawn renewed attention to the need for clearer pre-hike education and potentially enhanced signage at trailheads warning of cardiac and altitude risks. Details about the circumstances of the death were not fully disclosed, but the incident has reignited conversations within Colorado's outdoor recreation and public health communities.

Colorado's fourteeners collectively attract hundreds of thousands of visitors each year, and mountain rescue teams respond to dozens of medical emergencies on high peaks annually. Authorities have not yet announced specific policy changes stemming from the review.

topStory.headline: Trump Pledges 35-Race Campaign Blitz in Final Month Before Midterms as Some Republicans Distance Themselves From Party Convention
topStory.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Wednesday that he will spend the final 30 days before the November midterm elections campaigning across 35 competitive congressional and Senate races, pledging to personally stump for Republican candidates in tight contests. Speaking at a White House dinner in the Rose Garden attended by GOP members of Congress, Trump said he intends to visit each of the 35 locations and called explicitly for his supporters to vote as though he himself were on the ballot.

Among the races Trump cited are Sen. Dan Sullivan's re-election bid in Alaska and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton's Senate campaign against Democrat James Talarico. Several House Republicans who attended Wednesday's White House event face competitive November contests, including Reps. Derrick Van Orden of Wisconsin, Tom Barrett of Michigan, and Mike Collins of Georgia. Trump made clear he would focus his travel on candidates in genuine jeopardy, saying he would not campaign for incumbents leading by wide margins.

Trump's political operation, the super PAC MAGA Inc., currently holds more than $400 million in its war chest according to the latest campaign finance filings, and Republican candidates in close races are hoping a portion of those funds will be directed their way. Earlier Wednesday, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that while he personally is not on the ballot, he views the midterms as an opportunity to support his party, framing his planned travel in explicitly partisan terms.

At the same time, a significant number of Republican candidates are keeping their distance from an upcoming two-day GOP convention scheduled to begin September 9 in Dallas, where Trump and Vice President JD Vance are both expected to speak. A Politico survey of more than 70 Republican candidates and party officials found most were not planning to attend, with some citing prior commitments and others expressing concern that proximity to Trump's rhetoric could damage their standing with independent voters. Rep. Tom Barrett, one of the House members in a competitive race who attended Wednesday's White House dinner, told Politico he felt he would be more useful in his district than at the convention.

The Dallas convention, described by critics within the party as a 'waste of time' and dubbed 'Trump-a-palooza,' is the first GOP midterm convention in American history and carries entry costs ranging from $25,000 to $100,000 per member. Proceeds are directed to a nonprofit that is not required to disclose its donors. The event's combination of steep ticket prices, lack of formal party business, and Trump's unpredictable public statements has left many vulnerable Republicans weighing whether attendance poses more political risk than reward ahead of what is expected to be a contentious midterm cycle.
